questions.question: Under a periodic-review base-stock policy with order-up-to level $S$, constant lead time $l$, backlogging, $I_1=S$ and no orders outstanding initially, let $l\geq2$ and $k\geq l+1$. What does the gap $S-I_k$ between the order-up-to level and the inventory level $I_k$ at the start of period $k$ equal?
options: The backlog at the start of period $k$, which equals the demand not yet served.
Only the order placed at the start of period $k$, which equals $D_{k-1}$.
The units still on order, which equal the demand of periods $k-l,\dots,k-1$.
The total demand of periods $1,\dots,k-1$, since every demanded unit is reordered.

questions.question: Under a periodic-review base-stock policy with order-up-to level $S$, constant lead time $l$, backlogging, $I_1=S$ and no orders outstanding initially, the inventory level for $k\geq l+1$ is distributed as $I=S-X$, where $X$ is the lead-time demand. For an integer $j$, which expression equals $\mathbb{P}(I=j)$?
options: $\mathbb{P}(X=S-j)$
$\mathbb{P}(X=j-S)$
$\mathbb{P}(X=j)$
$\mathbb{P}(X\leq S-j)$

questions.question: A base-stock policy with level $S$, lead time $l=1$, backlogging, $I_1=S$ and no outstanding orders faces independent period demands with mean $2$ in odd periods and mean $4$ in even periods. Which statement about the start-of-period levels $I_k$, $k\geq2$, is correct?
options: $I_k=S-D_{k-1}$ fails, because orders no longer equal the previous demand.
Still $I_k=S-D_{k-1}$, but $\mathbb{E}[I_k]$ alternates between $S-2$ and $S-4$.
The $I_k$ are identically distributed, since each window holds one demand.
The inventory position drifts away from $S$, since orders lag the season.

questions.question: A base-stock policy with order-up-to level $S$ has lead time $l=0$, backlogging and iid demands $D_k$, and starts with $I_1=S$. What is the inventory level $I_k$ at the start of each period $k$?
options: $I_k=S-D_{k-1}$, the level after one period's demand.
$I_k=S-D_k$, so $I$ is distributed as $S-D$.
$I_k=S-(k-1)\,\mathbb{E}[D]$, falling as demand accumulates.
$I_k=S$ in every period, so $\mathbb{P}(I=S)=1$.

questions.question: Under a periodic-review base-stock policy with order-up-to level $S$, constant lead time $l$, backlogging, $I_1=S$ and no orders outstanding initially, let $l\geq2$ and let the iid demands have $\operatorname{Var}(D)>0$. For $k\geq l+1$, are the consecutive levels $I_k$ and $I_{k+1}$ independent?
options: Yes: the demands are iid, so levels built from them are independent too.
No, but only in the first $l$ periods; from $k\geq l+1$ on they are independent.
No: both windows contain $D_{k-l+1},\dots,D_{k-1}$, so they are positively correlated.
No: a large shared demand lowers one level and raises the other one.

questions.question: A base-stock policy with order-up-to level $S=10$ has lead time $l=4$, backlogging and iid period demands with $\mathbb{E}[D]=3$. In the long run (periods $k\geq l+1$), what is the mean inventory level $\mathbb{E}[I]$?

A base-stock policy with level $S=5$, lead time $l=3$, backlogging, $I_1=S$ and nothing on order initially faces iid demands taking each value in $\{0,1,2,3,4\}$ with positive probability. For $k\geq l+1$, which set is the set of possible values of the inventory level $I_k$?

Under a base-stock policy with level $S=2$ and backlogging, the lead-time demand $X$ has pmf $\mathbb{P}(X=0,1,2,3,4)=0.25,\,0.30,\,0.29,\,0.12,\,0.04$. For periods $k\geq l+1$, what is the probability $\mathbb{P}(I<0)$ that a period starts with a backlog?

A base-stock policy with $S=7$, lead time $l=2$, backlogging, $I_1=7$ and nothing on order initially sees demands $D_1,\dots,D_5=2,1,3,2,4$. What is the inventory level $I_5$ at the start of period $5$?

A base-stock policy with level $S=10$ has lead time $l=3$, backlogging, a clean start ($I_1=S$, nothing on order) and iid period demands with $\operatorname{Var}(D)=2$. For periods $k\geq l+1$, what is the variance of the inventory level $I_k$?

A base-stock system with level $S$, lead time $l\geq1$, iid demands and a clean start normally backlogs unmet demand; the lead-time demand $X$ satisfies $\mathbb{P}(X>S)>0$. If unmet demand were lost instead, what happens to the result $I\sim S-X$?
options: It still holds, because orders keep replacing demand one for one.
It still holds whenever $S\geq l\,\mathbb{E}[D]$, so that the mean level is not negative.
The pmf changes, but the mean level stays $S-l\,\mathbb{E}[D]$.
It fails: the level can no longer be negative, while $S-X<0$ whenever $X>S$.

questions.question: Under a base-stock policy with iid demands, backlogging and lead time $l\geq1$, the long-run level is $I=S-X$, with ready rate $\alpha$ and holding and backlog costs $h,b>0$ per unit. Which statement about raising the order-up-to level from $S$ to $S+1$ is correct?
options: The pmf of $I$ moves one unit right; $\alpha$ and $\mathbb{E}[I^+]$ cannot decrease, $\mathbb{E}[I^-]$ cannot increase.
The pmf of $I$ moves one unit right, so the ready rate $\alpha$ strictly increases for every $S$.
The pmf of $I$ moves one unit right, so the average cost $h\,\mathbb{E}[I^+]+b\,\mathbb{E}[I^-]$ cannot increase.
Only $\mathbb{E}[I]$ changes; $\mathbb{P}(I<0)$ stays the same because $X$ does not depend on $S$.

questions.question: Under a periodic-review base-stock policy with order-up-to level $S$, constant lead time $l$, backlogging, $I_1=S$ and no orders outstanding initially and iid demands, the fill rate $\beta=\mathbb{E}[\min\{D,I^+\}]/\mathbb{E}[D]$ treats the demand $D=D_k$ of a period $k\geq l+1$ as independent of that period's start level $I=I_k$. Why is this justified?
options: $I_k$ has the same distribution in every period, which makes it independent of demand.
The order placed at the start of period $k$ equals $D_k$, so the two effects cancel out.
$I_k$ depends only on $D_{k-l},\dots,D_{k-1}$, and these are independent of $D_k$.
It is an approximation: $D_k$ is part of the window of $I_k$, but its effect fades for long lead times.

questions.question: A base-stock policy with $S=2$, lead time $l=1$ and backlogging has iid demands with $\mathbb{P}(D=0)=0.6$, $\mathbb{P}(D=1)=0.3$, $\mathbb{P}(D=2)=0.1$. What is the long-run ready rate $\alpha$, the fraction of periods that end with $I_k'\geq0$?

A base-stock policy with $S=6$, lead time $l=2$ and backlogging has iid demands with $\mathbb{E}[D]=2.5$, and the expected backlog is $\mathbb{E}[I^-]=0.3$. Using $I=I^+-I^-$, what is the expected on-hand stock $\mathbb{E}[I^+]$ at the start of a period $k\geq l+1$?

A base-stock policy with $S=1$, lead time $l=1$ and backlogging has iid demands with $\mathbb{P}(D=0)=0.5$, $\mathbb{P}(D=1)=0.3$, $\mathbb{P}(D=2)=0.2$. What is the long-run fill rate $\beta=\mathbb{E}[\min\{D,I^+\}]/\mathbb{E}[D]$, to two decimals?

In a base-stock system with level $S$, lead time $l\geq2$, backlogging and a clean start, the demands all have mean $\mathbb{E}[D]$ and variance $\operatorname{Var}(D)$; consecutive demands have covariance $c>0$, while demands more than one period apart are uncorrelated. Which conclusion still holds for $k\geq l+1$?
options: $\operatorname{Var}(I_k)=l\operatorname{Var}(D)$
$I_k$ is distributed as $S$ minus the $l$-fold convolution of the demand pmf
$\mathbb{E}[I_k]=S-l\,\mathbb{E}[D]$
Levels $l$ periods apart, $I_k$ and $I_{k+l}$, are uncorrelated

questions.question: Consider base-stock systems with iid demands, lead time $l\geq1$, backlogging and a level $S<l\,\mathbb{E}[D]$, so that the long-run mean level satisfies $\mathbb{E}[I]<0$. Which conclusion holds for every such system?
options: More than half of the periods start with a backlog: $\mathbb{P}(I<0)>\tfrac{1}{2}$.
Every period starts with a backlog: $\mathbb{P}(I<0)=1$.
The expected backlog equals the mean shortfall: $\mathbb{E}[I^-]=l\,\mathbb{E}[D]-S$.
The expected backlog exceeds the expected on-hand stock: $\mathbb{E}[I^-]>\mathbb{E}[I^+]$.

questions.question: A base-stock policy with lead time $l=3$, backlogging and a clean start has iid demands with $\operatorname{Var}(D)=2$. For $k\geq l+1$, what is the covariance $\operatorname{Cov}(I_k,I_{k+2})$ of the levels two periods apart?

A base-stock policy with lead time $l=3$, backlogging, $I_1=S$ and nothing on order initially has iid demands with $\mathbb{P}(D=0)=0.4$. What is $\mathbb{P}(I_3=S)$, the probability that period $3$ starts at the full level $S$?
